slides.title: Voice playback isolates socially relevant decisions
body: **Comparative cognition** investigates how animals acquire, retain and use information, while accounting for differences in sensory access and natural behavior. McComb and colleagues tested wild African elephant families with recordings of human speech rather than confronting them with people.

The speakers repeated the same sentence, allowing voice categories to vary while verbal content remained comparable. Maasai men elicited stronger defensive bunching and investigative smelling than Kamba men; adult male Maasai voices also elicited stronger defenses than female or boy voices.

**Defensive bunching** is the formation of a tight protective group. Recorded voices were sufficient to change this collective response, but the experiments did not locate the neurons storing human-associated danger or establish comprehension of the sentence.

slides.title: Olfactory access permits food-quantity choices
body: Plotnik and colleagues presented captive Asian elephants with two opaque buckets containing sunflower seeds. **Olfaction**, the detection of airborne chemicals, supplied the information: locked perforated lids admitted odors while preventing visual inspection and access to the food.

The table was withdrawn after sampling, the lids were unlocked, and the elephant chose one bucket. Experimental seed quantities ranged from 4 to 24 g. Solid lids prevented successful discrimination, supporting an olfactory basis rather than guidance from visible food or other available cues.

This preparation separated sensory investigation from the choice action. Its results concern judgments about relative food amounts; they do not establish that elephants counted individual seeds or encoded an abstract numerical symbol.

figure.caption: Plotnik et al. (2019), Fig. 1(A–D). Odor sampling and subsequent bucket choice.

refs: Joshua M. Plotnik, Daniel L. Brubaker, Rachel Dale, Lydia N. Tiller, Hannah S. Mumby, Nicola S. Clayton (2019). Elephants have a nose for quantity. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 116: 12566-12571. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1818284116

slides.title: Quantity discrimination depends on relative difference
body: The seed experiment varied the **quantity ratio**, the smaller food amount relative to the larger amount. Elephants chose the greater amount more reliably when the amounts differed markedly, and their performance declined as the ratio approached equality.

Pairs with the same ratio but different total amounts tested whether overall food magnitude controlled performance. For example, the published experiment compared 4 versus 8 g with 12 versus 24 g. Total magnitude did not account for the choice pattern.

Metal-bucket and double-blind controls retained successful discrimination, reducing explanations based on residual plastic-container odor or experimenter guidance. Ratio dependence is consistent with approximate quantity assessment, but a learned comparison of odor strength remains possible; no numerical neurons were recorded.

slides.title: A trunk-held tool can interfere with food sampling
body: Foerder and colleagues offered Asian elephants suspended fruit and branches beyond ordinary trunk reach, together with movable objects and sticks. **Tool use** requires using an external object to alter the relationship between the animal and its goal, rather than merely handling it.

The elephants reached and sniffed toward the food but did not use sticks to retrieve it. This failure differed from the later successful use of a standing platform by the juvenile male Kandula. The authors proposed that holding a stick may obstruct the trunk’s simultaneous olfactory and tactile investigation.

The proposed sensory interference was not independently manipulated. Failure with a primate-style reaching tool therefore cannot be equated with an absence of physical problem-solving ability, but neither does it prove that sensory interference caused every failure.

slides.title: A movable platform increases effective reach
body: Kandula rolled a large plastic cube beneath suspended food, placed his forefeet on it and reached with his trunk. The cube changed his body position while leaving the trunk available for grasping. Its functional contribution was increased reach, not direct contact with the food.

The first successful sequence occurred after earlier object exploration without food retrieval. On subsequent sessions he repositioned the cube beneath changed food locations and also used it to investigate an elevated enrichment object and overhanging blossoms.

The authors described the initial solution as insight-like because an organized sequence appeared without a documented series of reinforced partial solutions. Earlier cube experience prevents concluding that the solution arose without learning, and the behavior does not reveal the underlying neural computation.

slides.title: Tool transfer tests more than one learned location
body: After successful cube use, Foerder and colleagues displaced it within the enclosure to test whether Kandula had learned only a fixed feeding location. He searched for the cube, moved it to the suspended reward and used it as a standing platform.

When the cube was hidden in a passageway, he retrieved it and later returned directly to the previously successful hiding location. Replacing the cube with a large tire also produced platform use, supporting transfer beyond one particular object.

These manipulations distinguish flexible object use from repeatedly standing at the original location. They still permit contributions from remembered rewards and prior manipulation experience. The evidence establishes behavioral flexibility in the tested individual, rather than a species-wide rate of insight or a causal memory circuit.

slides.title: Cooperation requires simultaneous control of a rope
body: Plotnik and colleagues adapted a **loose-rope cooperation task** for Asian elephants. One rope passed around a sliding food platform, with an end available to each partner. Pulling alone unthreaded the rope; coordinated holding and pulling brought the food within reach.

Initial single-rope training taught the pulling action. During paired testing the animals approached through separate lanes from 10 m away, while caretakers remained silent and looked away after release. These precautions reduced immediate human guidance without eliminating the elephants’ training history.

Successful simultaneous release established that the apparatus could be operated jointly. It did not alone establish that either animal understood the partner’s necessity, because both could simply repeat a previously rewarded pulling response upon reaching the rope.

slides.title: Delayed arrival requires inhibition of immediate pulling
body: **Response inhibition** means withholding an available action when acting immediately would prevent success. In delayed-release trials, the first elephant had to leave the rope available until its partner arrived rather than pull as soon as it reached the apparatus.

Training increased release delays in 5-s steps to 25 s. Tests then included previously untrained intervals of 26–45 s. Waiting succeeded on approximately 88–97% of trials across the lead elephants, and performance on longer delays improved after the first test day.

Transfer to longer intervals argues against one rigidly learned short waiting period. The preparation nevertheless involved shaping and repeated rewards, so successful waiting does not establish spontaneous cooperative understanding in an untrained animal or identify a specific inhibitory neuronal pathway.

slides.title: A partner’s presence is insufficient without rope access
body: The **no-rope control** left the partner present but placed its rope end out of reach. This separated social proximity from the partner’s ability to contribute mechanically. The lead elephant still had access to its own rope and could attempt to pull.

Most tested lead elephants reduced pulling when the partner lacked access, while normal joint trials remained successful. During delayed trials, pulling also increased after the partner arrived at the rope compared with the period before arrival.

The contrast supports sensitivity to conditions required for joint success, not merely another elephant’s presence. Feeling rope tension when the partner grasps it remains a possible learned cue. The results therefore do not require attributing intentions or a human-like theory of mind to the partner.

slides.title: Mirror access changes opportunities for self-investigation
body: Plotnik, de Waal and Reiss installed an elephant-accessible mirror measuring 244 by 244 cm. **Mirror self-recognition** is tested through behavior directed toward one’s own body using the reflection, rather than through attention to the mirror alone.

Baseline and covered-mirror phases established comparison behavior before the reflective surface was available. Elephants could approach and inspect the large mirror closely with their trunks, unlike earlier arrangements that kept a small reflective surface beyond reach.

All subjects developed mirror-associated testing and self-directed behavior, including unusual trunk and head movements and inspection of their mouths. The preparation makes bodily information available; exploration of a mirror by itself still cannot establish that an animal recognizes its reflected identity.

figure.caption: Plotnik et al. (2006), Fig. 1. Original accessible-mirror enclosure preparation.

refs: Joshua M. Plotnik, Frans B. M. de Waal, Diana Reiss (2006). Self-recognition in an Asian elephant. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 103: 17053-17057. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0608062103

slides.title: A sham mark controls touch and odor explanations
body: The **mark test** placed a visible mark on an otherwise unseen part of the elephant’s head. An invisible sham mark on the opposite side controlled for application-related tactile and olfactory cues, leaving visual appearance as the intended difference.

Happy repeatedly investigated the visible mark during or soon after mirror proximity, while the sham-mark side did not receive equivalent touching. Prior covered-mirror sham tests had not elicited mark-directed investigation. The other elephants explored the mirror but did not pass the mark test.

Selective touching supports using the reflection to obtain information about one’s own body. The result is individual-specific and does not establish the prevalence of mirror recognition in elephants or prove that all forms of self-awareness depend on this particular visual task.

slides.title: A positive mark test has a defined evidential scope
body: Happy’s head touching increased during the initial mark session, especially during mirror exposure or within 90 s after it. The temporal association matters because a purely tactile response to application would not specifically require visual access to the reflective surface.

The paper compared these responses with earlier open-mirror sessions and nonmirror conditions. Husbandry constraints prevented an ideal visible-mark, covered-mirror control while isolating the subject from its partner, leaving an explicitly acknowledged limitation in the design.

Mirror-guided self-investigation is evidence about processing bodily information. Its association with empathy or social complexity is a comparative hypothesis, not a demonstrated causal relationship in this experiment. Neither mirror behavior nor mark touching identified the responsible cortical cells.

slides.title: Body weight can obstruct a goal
body: Dale and Plotnik tested **body awareness**, the ability to treat one’s own body as a relevant object in a task. Asian elephants stood on a rubber mat while attempting to pass a stick to an experimenter in front of them.

In the test condition, a rope attached the stick to the mat. The elephant’s weight prevented the mat and attached stick from moving freely. Stepping off removed this obstruction and enabled the transfer, whereas an unattached-stick control permitted transfer without stepping off.

Elephants left the mat much more often when their weight obstructed the required action. The result concerns a functional body–environment relationship, not recognition of a visual identity, and should not be treated as the same assay as mirror self-recognition.

figure.caption: Dale & Plotnik (2017), Fig. 1. Original mat-and-stick transfer task.

refs: Rachel Dale, Joshua M. Plotnik (2017). Elephants know when their bodies are obstacles to success in a novel transfer task. Scientific Reports 7: 46309. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep46309

The crucial relation is mechanical: the elephant’s own weight maintains the constraint until it changes its body position.

slides.title: Discomfort differs from self-obstruction
body: A second control tested whether elephants stepped off the mat simply because pulling created an uncomfortable sensation under their feet. The animal transferred footwear sideways between experimenters while another experimenter tugged the mat’s attached rope.

The tug produced underfoot disturbance without making body weight an obstacle to the required transfer. Elephants left the mat less often in this control than in the attached-stick test, making discomfort alone an inadequate explanation of the test response.

The control does not reveal whether the animal explicitly conceptualized its own body. It supports a narrower account in which behavior distinguishes an obstructing body position from an irrelevant physical disturbance. Movement, tactile feedback and previous task learning remain components of that solution.

slides.title: Early success limits a repeated-training explanation
body: Across testing, elephants removed their weight from the mat far more often when the stick was attached than when it was unattached or when the mat was tugged during the discomfort control. The conditions therefore differed according to the task’s physical requirement.

The investigators separately examined the first test session because repeated trials could teach a specific escape response. Early successful transfers were common, and some occurred on the first trial, reducing the explanation that success required extensive training within the experiment.

Prior handling and transfer experience was not absent. The evidence supports practical sensitivity to self-obstruction under these conditions, while leaving open how the relationship was represented and whether it generalizes to novel body–object problems outside the tested setting.

slides.title: Von Economo neurons have a distinctive bipolar form
body: **Von Economo neurons**, or VENs, are identified here by an elongated spindle-shaped cell body with one large apical dendrite and one large basal dendrite, with little branching near the soma. **Dendrites** are neuronal processes that receive and integrate synaptic input.

Hakeem and colleagues examined postmortem elephant cortex using Nissl staining, which reveals cell bodies and cortical architecture. Cells with this morphology occurred in African elephant frontoinsular and dorsolateral frontal tissue and in Asian elephant anterior cingulate tissue.

Shape and regional location establish an anatomical cell category in these specimens. They do not measure synaptic input, firing rate or transmitter release. A proposal that these cells rapidly transmit socially important information remained an interpretation requiring direct physiological and connectional tests.

slides.title: Frontoinsular tissue concentrates VENs
body: The **frontoinsular cortex**, abbreviated FI, is a cortical region at the frontal–insular transition. Hakeem and colleagues mapped VEN locations in serial Nissl-stained sections rather than assigning cells from overall brain size or presumed social intelligence.

The largest elephant VEN concentration occupied tissue comparable in location to FI in humans and apes. VENs were more prevalent near gyral crowns and sparse near sulcal depths. A **gyrus** is a cortical fold’s raised part; a **sulcus** is the intervening groove.

Regional concentration and folding relationships support organized distribution rather than uniform scattering across cortex. The anatomical correspondence does not establish identical human and elephant functions, and no FI activity was recorded during social decisions in this study.

slides.title: ACC anatomy does not establish an empathy circuit
body: The **anterior cingulate cortex**, or ACC, lies on the medial cerebral surface. Hakeem and colleagues found VENs in subgenual anterior cingulate tissue and documented the same morphology in an Asian elephant ACC specimen, at lower density than in FI.

Earlier tissue removal limited mapping in parts of ACC and in one hemisphere. Such incomplete sampling matters when distinguishing a sparse population from an unexamined region. The paper’s regional descriptions are based on available histology, not a complete functional atlas.

Connections between ACC, social awareness and emotional evaluation were discussed largely from comparative human evidence. The elephant specimens establish cellular presence; they do not establish that ACC VENs are necessary for reassurance, cooperation or mirror-guided self-investigation.

Subgenual refers to a position beneath the genu, the curved anterior part of the corpus callosum; a regional analogy does not by itself prove functional equivalence.

slides.title: Frontal VENs extend beyond the frontoinsular region
body: Hakeem and colleagues also identified VENs in a **dorsolateral frontal** cortical area, located toward the upper outer frontal surface. The original photomicrograph includes both paired and isolated cells with elongated bodies and prominent opposing dendrites.

The investigators searched the frontal cortex in mounted stained sections, using cell morphology to identify candidate VENs. Additional small populations occurred in other frontal locations, so the reported specialization was not confined to one precisely bounded frontoinsular field.

This wider distribution complicates claims that one cell shape corresponds to a single social function. The study did not determine elephant-specific projection targets, neurotransmitter identities or response selectivity. Similar morphology across regions is evidence of a shared anatomical feature, not proof of identical circuitry.

slides.title: VENs concentrate in cortical layer five
body: A **cortical layer** is a band defined by differences in cell composition and arrangement through cortical depth. In the mapped elephant FI region, VENs occurred primarily in layer 5, alongside other large neurons with different shapes.

Serial sections and higher-magnification inspection connected cell morphology to laminar position. The authors also described dense clusters beneath the cortex as possible “claustral islands”; that identification was proposed from their location and appearance rather than established by tracing connections.

Laminar position provides a hypothesis about participation in cortical output, but does not reveal an elephant VEN’s exact target or synaptic effect. Neither the source’s section map nor its photomicrograph records active information flow through a social-decision circuit.

slides.title: Cell abundance differs from proportion within a region
body: **Stereology** estimates cell abundance from systematically sampled tissue rather than counting only conspicuous cells in a selected image. Hakeem and colleagues used this approach to estimate frontoinsular VEN numbers in the two hemispheres of one African elephant.

The estimates were approximately 10,200 VENs on the right and 9,110 on the left. The proportions differed more sharply: about 0.78% of counted neurons in the relevant right FI layers versus 2.6% on the left, which was smaller but more densely populated.

Absolute abundance and regional percentage therefore answer different questions. These estimates do not establish a population-wide hemispheric rule, greater intelligence on one side, or a relationship between an individual’s VEN number and its measured social behavior.

slides.title: Similar cell shapes suggest evolutionary convergence
body: **Convergent evolution** is the independent emergence of similar traits in lineages without a recent shared origin of that trait. Hakeem and colleagues compared elephant VEN morphology with cells reported in hominids and cetaceans and examined several other mammalian groups.

Comparable elongated cells occurred in the elephant material and the dolphin comparison, while the surveyed close relatives generally lacked comparable VEN populations. The authors proposed independent emergence associated with large brains and possibly demands for rapid long-distance information transmission.

The comparative distribution supports an evolutionary hypothesis, not a demonstrated conduction mechanism. Axon dimensions, connection targets and conduction times were not measured in the elephant cells. Nor does a shared cell shape establish equal cognitive capacities across these distantly related animals.

slides.title: Newborn cortex supplies developmental anatomy
body: Jacobs and colleagues examined cortical tissue from a stillborn African elephant and a newborn giraffe. The elephant brain weighed 1,745 g; these specimens represent an early developmental stage, not normal adult brain size or an adult cognitive performance comparison.

Samples came from elephant frontal, motor and occipital cortex, with anatomical locations documented before staining. Blocks were approximately 3–5 mm thick. Comparing defined regions reduced ambiguity about where the analyzed neuronal forms originated.

The design permits comparisons of cellular morphology across species and developmental datasets. The sampling outlines used adult brains because newborn specimens were fragmented; clinical history and fixation also limit inference. Newborn architecture cannot by itself identify the neural basis of the adult’s learned vocal repertoire or social experience.

slides.title: Golgi staining exposes whole dendritic configurations
body: The **Golgi method** impregnates a subset of neurons so that their cell bodies and dendritic branches can be examined against relatively unstained tissue. Jacobs and colleagues used a modified Golgi technique and computer-assisted tracing of newborn elephant cortical neurons.

Selection favored neurons whose processes could be followed and were not excessively obscured or truncated. The source’s motor-cortex tracings retain the positions of cell bodies relative to the pial surface, the outer cortical boundary. Different morphologies occupied overlapping rather than perfectly isolated depths.

Selective staining provides detailed shape information but is not a census of all cell types. An anatomical tracing neither establishes which synapses were functional nor measures electrical responses. Selected cells had to permit reliable tracing of branches within the tissue section.

slides.title: Flattened pyramidal cells broaden dendritic geometry
body: A **pyramidal neuron** typically has a prominent apical dendrite and several basal dendrites. Jacobs and colleagues described elephant forms whose apical dendrites bifurcated widely or extended laterally, including flattened pyramidal neurons distinct from a narrow upright configuration.

The newborn frontal material already contained multiple projection-neuron morphologies. Published tracings placed these forms within cortical depth and supported comparisons with ordinary pyramidal and inverted pyramidal cells, rather than assuming one canonical cortical shape.

A wider dendritic configuration could sample inputs over a different tissue extent, but the study did not map the actual presynaptic partners. Morphological diversity is established; a particular role in elephant social learning, vocal imitation or behavioral flexibility is not established by these images.

slides.title: Multipolar forms enlarge the cortical cell repertoire
body: **Multipolar neurons** have several processes extending from the cell body rather than one dominant apical and one basal dendrite. The newborn elephant frontal tissue contained nonpyramidal multipolar forms alongside inverted pyramidal, flattened pyramidal and other configurations.

Jacobs and colleagues documented these cells in Golgi photomicrographs and traced their dendritic trees. The photomicrographs preserve the actual tissue appearance, while the source’s companion reconstructions aid comparisons of branching geometry and cortical position.

The study reported greater morphological variety among elephant projection cells than in the newborn giraffe material. This is a comparison of sampled stained neurons, not an experimental demonstration that each additional shape supplies a distinct cognitive operation. Axonal targets and activity during behavior remain unresolved.

slides.title: Dendritic spines vary with cell type and development
body: **Dendritic spines** are small protrusions on dendrites that commonly receive synaptic contacts. Jacobs and colleagues measured spine distributions along traced dendritic segments, using **spine density** to describe the number of visible spines per unit dendritic length.

Several newborn local-circuit morphologies carried spines despite comparatively aspiny adult counterparts. The source compared spine-density profiles by cell type and distance from the soma, revealing that developing neuronal surface organization is not simply a scaled-down adult configuration.

Visible spines are structural observations, not measurements of synaptic strength, release probability or receptor composition. The authors discussed maturation of presumed inhibitory and excitatory classes comparatively, but transmitter identity and functional inhibition were not established by the Golgi staining itself.

slides.title: Projection dendrites continue growing after birth
body: **Total dendritic length** sums the lengths of the traced branches in a neuronal tree. Jacobs and colleagues compared newborn elephant cells with previously collected adult material using a matched subset of neuronal types.

Adult projection cells had more extensive dendrites: reported total lengths were approximately 32% greater for pyramidal, 36% greater for flattened pyramidal and 30% greater for nonpyramidal multipolar neurons. In contrast, the compared interneuron dendritic lengths were not similarly enlarged in adults.

These cross-sectional differences support prolonged growth of projection-neuron dendritic systems. They do not track the same cells through development, and they cannot separate maturation from particular social or sensory experiences. Structural growth should not be equated automatically with a measured increase in cognitive competence.

slides.title: An African elephant copied environmental sounds
body: **Vocal production learning** is modification of the sounds an animal produces through experience of an acoustic model. Poole and colleagues recorded truck-like calls from Mlaika, an adolescent African elephant whose night enclosure was approximately 3 km from a major highway.

Her imitations resembled recorded truck sounds in duration and fundamental-frequency characteristics while differing from ordinary African elephant calls. **Fundamental frequency** is the repetition rate underlying a periodic vocal sound, represented by its lowest harmonic when detectable.

The calls were no more similar to simultaneously recorded trucks than to trucks recorded at other times, favoring imitation of general acoustic features rather than exact immediate copying. The case establishes an unusual learned production pattern, not its neural pathway or prevalence in wild elephants.

slides.title: Long-term companions can supply a heterospecific model
body: **Heterospecific imitation** copies a sound associated with another species. Poole and colleagues described Calimero, an African male elephant that had lived for 18 years with Asian female elephants and produced chirp-like sounds unusual for African elephants.

His chirps resembled the Asian models in acoustic comparisons and differed from ordinary African adult, adolescent and calf calls. The authors analyzed duration and frequency-related properties, rather than relying only on a listener’s impression that the calls sounded similar.

Long-term social exposure is consistent with learning a companion-associated vocal pattern. The record was not a randomized exposure experiment, so it does not establish that social bonding caused the change or that every African elephant would imitate chirps under comparable housing conditions.

slides.title: Acoustic controls distinguish imitation
body: The Poole study compared imitations with both their proposed models and ordinary elephant vocalizations. Including adult, adolescent and calf calls reduced the explanation that an unusual imitation was simply an age-related or sex-related member of the normal repertoire.

Mlaika’s truck-like calls occupied acoustic space near truck sounds, whereas Calimero’s chirp-like calls resembled Asian chirps. The published multidimensional comparisons summarize combinations of acoustic features; their axes are not anatomical brain dimensions or measures of intelligence.

Evidence of acoustic matching supports experience-related flexibility in vocal production. It does not identify whether changes were learned through spontaneous practice, reinforcement or another route. The authors’ social-bond hypothesis explains a possible adaptive function, while the measured result remains the altered call structure.

slides.title: Imitation suggests a possible social function
body: Elephant **fission–fusion societies** involve groups that separate and reunite while maintaining longer-lasting relationships. Poole and colleagues proposed that vocal convergence could help sustain individual-specific bonds when companions are not continuously together.

Calimero’s resemblance to Asian companions supplies a social context for this proposal, whereas Mlaika’s truck imitation establishes flexibility beyond ordinary social calls. Neither case manipulated bond strength or measured a subsequent improvement in recognition or affiliation.

A capacity and its evolutionary function are different claims. The documented imitations establish learned acoustic flexibility in particular elephants. Selection for maintaining social contact remains a plausible adaptive explanation, requiring evidence that the resulting vocal changes affect communication or relationships in natural groups.

slides.title: Koshik modified his vocal tract with his trunk
body: Stoeger and colleagues analyzed Koshik, an Asian elephant producing speech-like Korean sounds. He inserted his trunk tip into his mouth from the right and raised his lower jaw during phonation. **Phonation** is production of the periodic source sound by the vocal apparatus.

Trunk insertion occurred about 0.3 s before vocal onset, and removal about 0.4 s after vocalization. The coordinated movement changed the vocal-tract configuration rather than simply emitting an ordinary elephant call in response to a spoken command.

The authors inferred that the trunk helped overcome anatomical constraints on vowel production. Without internal imaging they could not determine whether tongue movements also contributed. The external movement sequence was documented together with measured acoustic changes.

slides.title: Spectral structure separates pitch from vowel quality
body: **Formants** are resonant frequency bands shaped by the vocal tract; they contribute to vowel quality. Fundamental frequency instead reflects the periodic source. Stoeger and colleagues compared both properties in Koshik’s imitations and Korean human utterances.

The word-like utterance “nuo” was recorded from a trainer, Koshik and an independent Korean speaker. Narrow-band and wide-band spectrograms retained the different information needed to distinguish harmonics from broader resonance patterns, with F1 and F2 marked in the original panels.

Matching formants requires control beyond simply producing a similar pitch. The recordings support detailed acoustic imitation, while not establishing that the elephant understood the human utterance’s meaning or that an elephant vocal tract normally produces the same vowels without modification.

slides.title: Learned utterances differ from natural Asian calls
body: Stoeger and colleagues compared Koshik’s imitations with natural Asian elephant vocalizations recorded from animals of different ages and sexes in captive and wild settings. Duration, fundamental-frequency extremes and the first spectral peak or formant supplied acoustic comparison measures.

The imitations grouped with human model utterances and differed strongly from the natural Asian elephant calls. This control addresses the explanation that trainers merely assigned word labels to ordinary calls already present in the species’ repertoire.

The acoustic contrast supports production learning of a human-associated sound pattern. It does not establish how many other elephants could learn it, and the observed similarity does not determine which auditory or motor neurons are necessary to perceive, practice or reproduce the sounds.

slides.title: Blind listening reveals better vowels than consonants
body: Native Korean listeners transcribed Koshik’s recordings without being told the trainers’ proposed spellings or meanings. This **blind transcription** reduced the possibility that a suggested word would determine what listeners reported hearing.

The analysis supported five word-like imitations, with much better agreement for vowels than consonants: approximately 67% versus 21% overall. The trainers’ labels therefore did not correspond to equally accurate reproduction of every speech component.

The asymmetry fits the formant-matching evidence and places a concrete limit on imitation fidelity. Recognition by human listeners is an acoustic outcome, not proof of semantic understanding by the elephant. A remembered sound can be copied without representing the referent or instruction associated with a human word.

slides.title: Formants require sensory–motor coordination
body: Koshik’s first two formants for commonly produced vowels resembled those of his trainers, despite the elephant’s much longer unmodified vocal tract. The observed trunk–mouth configuration supplied a distinctive way of adjusting the resonant filter during controlled sound production.

Matching a heard target requires a relationship between acoustic perception and motor output. The paper inferred transfer of auditory information to planning systems controlling phonation and trunk movement, based on the precision of the behavior and acoustic match.

That relationship is a functional inference, not a mapped elephant neural circuit. The study did not trace cortical projections or manipulate neurotransmitters, receptors or ion channels. A specific songbird-like pathway cannot be assigned to elephants from successful imitation alone.

slides.title: Older matriarchs discriminate familiarity
body: McComb and colleagues played female contact calls to wild African elephant families whose association histories were known. An **association index** describes how often families encountered one another, supplying a behavioral measure of caller familiarity independent of the immediate playback response.

Families led by older matriarchs differentiated low- and high-association callers more sharply. The published curves compare representative matriarch ages of 35 and 55 years; the analysis treated age continuously rather than as only two fixed categories.

Greater discrimination cannot be reduced to uniformly lower defensiveness in older-led groups. The study supports accumulated social knowledge, but age was not experimentally assigned. Experience, survival history and family characteristics remain relevant when interpreting why older leadership was associated with better discrimination.

slides.title: Social knowledge influences group responses
body: **Social recognition** distinguishes individuals or relationship categories from available cues. In the Amboseli playback study, contact-call familiarity predicted both defensive bunching and investigative smelling, linking acoustic identity information to coordinated protective behavior.

The investigators considered group composition, calf-related variables and the ages of females other than the matriarch. The association with matriarch age persisted beyond these measured alternatives, and older-led families were also associated with higher reproductive performance in the observational records.

These results connect social information with group-level consequences but do not demonstrate that one matriarch stores every member’s knowledge. They also do not locate a memory trace in FI, ACC or any other structure. Behavioral leadership and anatomical specialization remain different forms of evidence.

slides.title: Experienced leadership distinguishes predator categories
body: McComb and colleagues used lion-roar playbacks to distinguish judgments about predator number from judgments about predator category. Three lions elicited stronger defensive responses than one, consistent with assessment of the scale of an approaching threat.

Sensitivity to male rather than female lion roars increased with matriarch age. Older matriarchs and their groups devoted stronger listening and defensive responses to the category associated with greater danger to elephants, rather than responding equally strongly to all lion sounds.

Different threat features therefore showed different relationships with experience. Playback isolates the acoustic stimulus, while observational age comparisons leave the acquisition route unresolved. The study did not establish that older matriarchs possess a generally superior sensory threshold or identify a predator-category neuron.

slides.title: Voice resynthesis tests which acoustic cues are sufficient
body: McComb and colleagues resynthesized human voices so that fundamental frequency and formant values resembled those of the opposite sex. This manipulation tested whether those prominent acoustic properties alone accounted for the elephants’ differential responses to men and women.

Defensive reactions retained the original direction: male-origin voices still elicited stronger responses despite the modified pitch and formant pattern. The experiment therefore did not support a simple classification rule based only on those two manipulated features.

Other retained acoustic characteristics could carry information about the original speaker category. The results support flexible auditory risk assessment but do not identify every effective cue. They also do not show that elephants use the same representation or linguistic categories that human listeners assign to the voices.

slides.title: Social disruption has long-lasting behavioral correlates
body: Shannon and colleagues compared Amboseli families with a Pilanesberg population founded by young elephants translocated after culling. **Social disruption** involved loss of older family members and a break in normal opportunities to acquire socially relevant information.

Contact-call playbacks and resynthesized calls tested familiarity and caller-age-related dominance cues. Amboseli responses were adjusted to social category and age-related information; Pilanesberg families did not show the same appropriate pattern of discrimination decades after the founding disturbance.

The comparison supports lasting consequences associated with disrupted social history. It was not a randomized culling experiment, and differences between locations and population histories remain possible contributors. No brain lesion, synaptic alteration or hormone pathway was directly measured by these playback responses.

slides.title: Bystanders contact distressed companions
body: Plotnik and de Waal observed captive Asian elephants after naturally occurring distress and compared behavior with matched control periods. **Affiliative contact** is nonaggressive social contact, including trunk touches directed toward another animal’s head, mouth or other body regions.

Bystanders contacted the distressed animal sooner and more frequently during post-distress observations than during matched periods. Bystander initiation mattered because it separated another animal’s approach from contact elicited solely by the distressed elephant actively seeking company.

The pattern supports reassurance as a behavioral description. The observers did not measure the recipient’s subjective state, establish that contact reduced physiological stress, or test a causal role for oxytocin, dopamine or a particular cortical population. Functional and neural interpretations remain narrower than the observed contact pattern.

slides.title: Rapid affiliation supports reassurance
body: The reassurance study concentrated first affiliative contacts within the first minute after distress, compared with matched control observations. **Emotional contagion** describes a proposed sharing of another individual’s state; synchronized distress-related behavior among bystanders supplied behavioral evidence consistent with that interpretation.

Physical contacts and vocal responses were recorded separately. This distinguished changes in approach or touch from changes in calling and allowed the timing of affiliation to be compared against ordinary social interaction rather than merely noting that elephants sometimes touched one another.

Coordinated behavior is compatible with social-state sensitivity, but does not establish a specific internal emotion or its neural cause. Together, the cognition, imitation and anatomy studies support multiple specialized capacities while leaving the causal circuits linking elephant experience, cellular physiology and social decisions largely untested.

items.text: Olfactory quantity judgments and alternative tool tasks reveal capacities that a visual or trunk-held task can miss.
Partner-access controls, sham marks and nonobstructing-mat controls distinguish specific contingencies from simple alternative explanations.
African imitations and Koshik’s acoustic matching establish flexible sound production; they do not establish human language comprehension.
VEN morphology, regional distribution and developing dendritic architecture are established anatomical findings; their exact social functions remain untested.
Older-led groups discriminate socially relevant calls and predator categories more finely; disrupted social histories are associated with persistent deficits.
Reassurance, recognition and cooperation are behavioral findings; no cited study establishes a complete elephant social circuit or its necessary transmitter mechanism.
